articles.title: UK interest rate rise: Three ways it could affect you
articles.summary: Job, loans and savings are all affected by the rise in interest rates announced by the Bank of England.
articles.body:
Interest rates have been raised for the first time in more than three years - and it could be good and bad news for you.

Here are three ways the increase to 4% from 3.75% could affect you.

Rate-setters at the Bank make changes to interest rates to fulfil their role of keeping price rises at a steady level.

Higher rates are meant to encourage people to spend less, reducing demand for goods and services and limiting price rises.

This impacts businesses in two ways - less money to spend among their customers may mean they sell less, but also the cost of borrowing to invest as a company goes up.

Many businesses, particularly small ones, have variable rate loans which are influenced by the Bank rate.

Firms say higher rates limit their ability to offer new jobs and wage rises.

Mitchell Barnes, founder and chief executive of Ryse 3D, which manufactures 3D parts for the defence and automotive sectors, said the "reality" of rising interest rates was to look at the cost of employees and people.

That could include greater use of robots rather than workers.

"It's going to cause issues with, I suppose, employment across all sectors for people," he said.

"You're going to see reduced employment, more automation, more robotics being put into facilities, just in order to increase efficiency and make that money go further."

The Bank rate - and where it is expected to go in future - has a significant impact on the interest rates customers are offered on savings products.

So, if you're saving up for something quite expensive, like a holiday, or very expensive, like a home, then a rate rise could be good news.

When interest rates were low throughout the 2010s, the returns for savers were poor, but borrowing costs were low too.

The answer then and now, according to experts, is to make sure you move your savings to benefit from the best possible rates.

What's happening to UK interest rates and what does it mean for mortgages?

You need £17,000 for a first home - here's how to save it

Faisal Islam: How high will interest rates go?

Leaving your savings in an old account (a product not offered to new customers), rather than shopping around, can mean you are penalised for your loyalty.

"Savers have endured years of unrewarded loyalty, with those leaving [a £20,000 cash pot] in closed accounts losing out on an extra £139 over the past three years compared to on-sale easy access accounts," said Rachel Springall, from financial information service Moneyfacts.

She also said locking away your money for longer, with a fixed-term deal, is usually more lucrative.

The other flipside is that renting while you save could get more expensive, because a rising Bank rate may well increase costs for landlords.

The big losers from a rate rise are those who borrow money, and specifically those on variable rate mortgages.

About 500,000 homeowners have a mortgage that "tracks" the Bank of England's rate.

Any rise in the Bank rate means an increase in the monthly repayments on their outstanding loan. For a typical loan, the cost is going up by about £31 a month now the Bank has raised the base rate, but it depends on the size of people's loans.

An additional 500,000 homeowners on standard variable rates (SVRs) must wait to see if their lender chooses to pass on any Bank rate rise. Typically, this would mean a £14 increase per month in repayments for a 0.25 percentage points rates rise.

If you, like 87% of mortgage-holders, have a fixed-rate deal, then the payments will stay the same until the end of your current deal, which is usually two or five years.

While monthly payments are not immediately affected by a rate change, future deals are. Lenders had already "priced in" the latest rate rise when quoting new deals. Expectations for the Bank rate into next year are crucial on what they offer next.

The average rate on fixed deals are much higher now than was predicted at the start of the year. It means those remortgaging, possibly after the post-Covid boom in the housing market, are facing the prospect of higher mortgage payments.

Some people have been choosing to move onto tracker deals instead, taking a view - including some risk - of the Bank rate not moving towards a series of further hikes.

articles.title: Centre amends Immigration and Foreigners (Exemption) Order: What Indians travelling to or returning from Nepal or Bhutan need to know
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The ministry of home affairs (MHA) on Thursday notified the Immigration and Foreigners (Exemption) (Amendment) Order, 2026, introducing
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The ministry of home affairs (MHA) on Thursday notified the Immigration and Foreigners (Exemption) (Amendment) Order, 2026, introducing specific amendments to the Immigration and Foreigners (Exemption) Order, 2025.Under the amended order, Indian nationals travelling to or returning from Nepal or Bhutan by land or air will be required to produce any one of the identity documents specified in the visa manual before an immigration officer. They will also have to furnish any information sought by the officer.The exemption provided under this clause shall not apply to a citizen of India departing to or returning from countries other than Nepal or Bhutan through the Indo-Nepal or Indo-Bhutan border by land or by air. In all such cases, they shall be required to possess a valid passport and their exit from or entry into India shall be only through the designated immigration posts.Citizens of Nepal or Bhutan entering or leaving IndiaUnder the new order, citizens of Nepal and Bhutan entering or leaving India by land or air will also be required to produce any one of the identity documents specified in the visa manual before an immigration officer. They will also have to provide any information sought by the officer.However, this exemption will not apply to citizens of Nepal or Bhutan entering or leaving India from or to a country other than Nepal or Bhutan.The exemption will also not apply to those who have boarded a flight or transited through China, Macau, Hong Kong or Pakistan. In such cases, they must possess both a valid passport and a valid visa.In both cases, citizens of Nepal and Bhutan must possess a valid passport and a valid visa.Who all are exemptedThe order also specifies categories of people exempted from the requirements to possess a valid passport or other travel document and visa for entering, staying in or exiting India.(a) Members of the Indian Navy, Army and Air Force travelling to or from India on official duty. Their family members accompanying them on government transport are also covered.(b) Registered Sri Lankan Tamil nationals who took shelter in India on or before January 9, 2015. They must be registered with an officer designated by the Central or state government.(c) Foreign crew members of military vessels, including warships and other government ships operated for non-commercial purposes, visiting India for repairs. They must have a Military Ship Repair Permit issued by an immigration officer at a designated immigration post and carry valid military identity documents.(d) Tibetans who entered India after 1959 but before May 30, 2003, with an Entry Permit issued by the Indian Embassy in Kathmandu. The exemption also covers those who entered India after May 30, 2003, with a Special Entry Permit issued by the embassy and through a designated immigration post on the India-Nepal border.(e) Members of minority communities — Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis and Christians — from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan who were forced to seek shelter in India due to religious persecution or fear of persecution, provided they entered India on or before December 31, 2024.What is a 'visa manual'The order defined the document as a manual issued by the central government from time to time, containing instructions on visas, immigration and related matters.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Why Trump’s got capitol punishment
articles.summary: Perfect storm: High cost of living, unpopular war, weak candidates Donald Trump, as he had wanted voters to think, was on the ballot in these US midterms.
articles.body: Perfect storm: High cost of living, unpopular war, weak candidatesDonald Trump, as he had wanted voters to think, was on the ballot in these US midterms. And that was the problem.Democrats won back both the House and the Senate by breaking through in states where Republican victories had become routine, including Texas, Kansas and South Carolina. This was a defeat that reached well beyond the usual battlegrounds.So, what happened? A perfect storm against Trumpism. Several failures reinforced one another: persistently high living costs, an unpopular war, candidates whose presidential backing could not overcome their weaknesses, an electorate seeking stronger checks on Trump, and concerns over corruption in high places. And Trump's dominance of the Republican Party made it harder for its candidates to escape responsibility for his record.Price, Price, BabyNearly nine in 10 voters identified living costs as a crucial or major consideration, according to SSRS exit polls reported by Reuters. Two-thirds blamed Trump for high prices; 62% disapproved of his performance. These figures measure voter perceptions, but perceptions of who is responsible are central to an election fought over affordability.Look at the economic numbers. September's inflation rate was 3.7%. Energy prices were 20.4% higher than a year earlier. These were highly visible costs households encountered repeatedly. Trump had set himself a demanding political test by promising rapid relief. So, all Democrats needed was for prices to remain painfully high after he had promised to bring them down.Nobody loved this warThe Iran war compounded the failure on inflation. It added an overseas commitment to a presidency built on promises to concentrate on American interests. And rising fuel costs connected foreign policy directly to domestic hardship.Before polling day, an AP-NORC survey found that roughly two-thirds of registered voters counted the Iran war among their leading election issues. Only 69% of Republican voters approved of Trump's foreign policy performance.And given that Trump had spent about $50 billion on the war, Democrats asked why Trump was promising relief at home while committing so much abroad.Trump hired, voters firedHis candidate choices aggravated national headwinds. But winning over Republican primary voters and persuading a broader electorate are two different things.In Texas, he backed attorney general Ken Paxton over incumbent Senator John Cornyn, a safer choice. Paxton lost. So did Trump-backed Senate candidates in North Carolina, South Carolina and Michigan.North Carolina illustrated this particularly clearly. Democrats fielded Roy Cooper, a former two-term governor with statewide recognition. Republicans put up Michael Whatley, a political operative who had never held elective office. Cooper campaigned on food and energy costs.That coalition is so 2024The so-called Trump social coalition was blown out of the water. His 2024 gains among younger and Hispanic voters were all but wiped away.The AP Voter Poll found that approximately seven in 10 voters under 30 backed Democratic House candidates, as did about six in 10 Hispanic voters.Warning signs preceded election day. Pew's late September to early October survey put Trump's approval among Latino registered voters at 24%, down from 38% in February 2025. Among those who said they had voted for him in 2024, approval had fallen from 93% to 57%.Anger beat apathyBefore the election, about three-quarters of Democratic-registered voters told AP-NORC that voting was "extremely" important, against roughly six in 10 Republicans. That was a warning about mobilisation.Trump tried to overcome the problem by making himself the centre of the campaign. But that just reminded dissatisfied voters who the problem guy was.He had asked Americans to trust his ability to deliver prosperity. When that failed to arrive, the party he had built around himself had little room to argue that responsibility belonged elsewhere.Trumpers to never-TrumpersEarly signs of Trumpism losing its sheen, even among some faithful supporters, look to be a pivotal factor.Some of the sharpest criticism came from people who had once defended Trump most fiercely. Former Republican congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene accused him of betraying his America First promises, particularly over Iran, healthcare and the Epstein files.Conservative commentator Tucker Carlson said he was leaving the Republican Party over its foreign policy direction.This guy's out of controlEconomic dissatisfaction also became a demand for institutional checks. The AP Voter Poll found that about seven in 10 voters wanted Congress to do more to check presidential power. That included four in 10 Republicans.Corruption was a major concern. Democrats gave dissatisfied voters something achievable: a legislature able to challenge the White House.Voters gave the party exactly that.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Comber: Investigation into 'major fish kill' underway after pollution incident
articles.summary: The pollution caused the death of brown and migratory sea trout in the Inler river.
articles.body:
A investigation is underway after "a major fish kill" in a County Down river, the Department for Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (Daera) has confirmed.

The pollution caused the death of brown and migratory sea trout in the Gransha, Ballystockart and Inler (also known as Enler) Rivers.

Glenn McKibbin, the secretary of Inler Angling Club, said about 1,000 fish were killed in the incident and it "could not have happened in a worse location on the river or at a worse time".

The Northern Ireland Environment Agency (NIEA) and Daera Inland Fisheries are working to "identify the source of the pollution and to finalise the numbers of fish killed".

The Department said the incident was reported by a member of the public on Tuesday at 09:30 GMT.

McKibbin said that "current and future fish stocks obliterated for years to come".

He added that resident and non-resident migratory fish, which only return at this of year to spawn, have been impacted.

"Knock-on effects for other wildlife such as resident kingfishers, herons & otters unavoidable.

"For our members and volunteers who work tirelessly in a bid to improve the river this is soul-destroying, particularly as the river was still in recovery from major pollution incidents / fish kills in 2013 and 2015," McKibbin said.

"Waterways up and down the country continue to be treated like sewers.

"The paltry fines that usually follow incidents of this nature are not a deterrent and the current 'system' is broken."

Many migratory fish, such as trout and salmon, swim up smaller tributaries to lay their eggs in cleaner, gravel-bottomed, or cooler waters away from larger predators in the main river.

A tributary is a smaller river that flows into a larger mainstem river where many migratory fish, such as trout and salmon, swim up to lay their eggs away from larger predators in the main river.

Inler Angling Club Chairperson David Pyper said: "For those who dedicate so much time and effort to caring for the river, witnessing the sheer loss of fish in circumstances such as these is particularly disappointing.

"The club hopes that the forthcoming investigations will establish the cause of this latest incident and help ensure appropriate steps are taken to protect the river and its wildlife."

The club has encouraged local representatives and authorities to continue to prioritise rivers and direct resources towards improving water quality and preventing further incidents.

articles.title: Multiple flights in Europe diverted because of bomb threats
articles.summary: At least 11 planes from cities, including Dublin, Madrid, and Warsaw, were diverted or grounded over bomb threats that have been determined to be unfounded.
articles.body: Multiple planes across Europe were diverted and forced to make emergency landings Thursday because of bomb threats that have turned out to be unfounded. At least 11 planes, originating from cities including Copenhagen, Dublin, Helsinki, Madrid, Milan and Warsaw, have been affected. The source of the threats was not immediately clear. These incidents came after several flights in Europe received similar warnings on Tuesday that the U.K. government described as "malicious hoax threats." "Upon receiving a threat regarding the placement of an improvised explosive device on board 4 aircraft heading to Prague, we are preparing with colleagues from Prague Airport for their landing. We assess the relevance of the threats as low," Czech Police wrote on X, before adding that inspections of the planes yielded "negative results." The threats come at a time when European officials have been blaming Russia and Iran for "hybrid attacks" and acts of sabotage, which both Moscow and Tehran deny, Reuters reported. RUSSIA'S SHADOW WAR IS PUTTING EUROPE ON EDGE AS GERMANY CONFRONTS A GROWING THREAT Earlier, a flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to a military air base in western France because of a bomb threat, according to French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu’s office. That flight landed safely at the base in Evreux in Normandy, with all 151 passengers and six crew members disembarking, the office said. A LOT Polish Airlines flight from Warsaw to Brussels landed at its destination, where inspections found no hazardous or suspicious items, the airline said. A Wizz Air flight from Milan to Bucharest landed safely in Bucharest following a bomb threat, according to airport spokesperson Teo Postelnicu. FRENCH SUPERMARKETS FACE MILLIONS IN LOSSES AFTER CYBERATTACK HITS REFRIGERATORS NATIONWIDE Finnair said that Flight 1761 from Helsinki to Rome was targeted by a bomb threat, but nothing was found after it landed in the Italian capital. Three Ryanair flights bound for Sofia, Bulgaria, had to make emergency landings because of bomb threats on board. articles.title: Football fan tried to stop Huntingdon train attack, jury hears
articles.summary: Stephen Crean says his grapple with the attacker was "like Come Dancing, we were all over the place".
articles.body:
A football fan who tried to stop the man accused of trying to kill 10 people on a train said the attacker was "on a mission", a court heard.

Stephen Crean said he attempted to stop Anthony Williams from using a knife on a train, which had to make an unscheduled stop in Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, on 1 November last year.

Cambridge Crown Court heard Crean describe his grapple with Williams as "like Come Dancing, we were all over the place", before he called 999 from a locked toilet.

Williams, 33, of Langford Road in Peterborough, denies 10 counts of attempted murder, and four other alleged attempted murders in earlier incidents in Peterborough and London.

Jurors have already heard accounts from five people Williams is accused of attempting to murder, on the York to London King's Cross LNER service, which had just left Peterborough station.

In a video recorded interview played to the court, Crean said he remembered choosing his carriage deliberately "because I knew it wasn't far from the buffet car" and he bought a meal deal for £6.

He recalled a young girl who ran past him saying there was a man with a "big knife".

Jurors have been shown CCTV footage that shows Crean was by a door of the buffet car when he encountered Williams.

Crean said Williams asked him, "Do you want to die?", adding that he "pulled out a blade from nowhere", describing it as "quite a big kitchen knife, I'll never forget it".

He said people were "struggling to get the buffet door shut", but when he "heard it click, happy days, then I went towards him [Williams]".

Crean, who was wearing Nottingham Forest clothing, said he grappled with Williams to "stop him" using the knife.

He said his fingers were cut and Williams was "twisting and turning" the knife.

After becoming free, Crean said he managed to lock himself in a toilet, adding: "I smiled, then middle-fingered him, then closed the door."

He then called 999 "probably for the first time in my life", and only came out when he heard the police walkie-talkies.

Asked about how Williams appeared, Crean said: "100% he was fine, he looked normal, he was just on a mission, he didn't seem angry."

Williams is also accused of attempting to murder Raza Aslam, Sachin Balakrishnan, Scott Bletcher, Kevin Deely, Scott Green, Jonathan Gjoshe, Michael Paffett, David Presland and Samir Zitouni on the London-bound train between Peterborough and Huntingdon on 1 November.

Prosecutors further allege that on 31 October, Williams tried to kill three people in Peterborough, before attempting to murder a teenager in the early hours of 1 November on a DLR train in east London.

Whether Williams carried out the attacks is not in question - the court has been told - but jurors must consider whether he intended to kill.

articles.title: University of Michigan students rally behind Abdul El-Sayed after his Senate win over Mike Rogers
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed's Michigan Senate win sparked celebration at the University of Michigan, where young voters say cost of living drove turnout.
articles.body: ANN ARBOR, Mich. — University of Michigan students galvanized around Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed following his defeat of Republican challenger Mike Rogers in Michigan's high-stakes U.S. Senate race. "Everyone's excited," said Affaan Shaik, a freshman studying pre-med at the University of Michigan. "Everyone I've spoken to, everyone I've seen — like last night we were all watching the election," Shaik added. "And everyone’s just rooting for Abdul, and that’s the vibe right now." 30% OF COLLEGE STUDENTS SAY VIOLENCE ACCEPTABLE WAY TO STOP SPEAKERS ON CAMPUSES, SURVEY FINDS The Ann Arbor campus recently made headlines after a video went viral showing a conservative Jewish activist being tackled to the ground during an open campus discussion. Lizzy Benichou was hosting a free-speech event on campus when a heated argument over Islam and Iranian women's rights turned physical. Video captured a female student shoving Benichou to the ground and kicking her before campus police intervened and took the student into custody. The confrontation underscored the contentious political and cultural climate surrounding higher education during the campaign cycle. However, El-Sayed’s victory demonstrated his ability to overcome Republican attempts to cast him as the poster child for far-left Democratic policies. ABDUL EL-SAYED DELIVERS MAJOR BLOW TO GOP IN MICHIGAN AFTER BRUISING SENATE RACE In his victory speech in Detroit early Wednesday morning, El-Sayed targeted the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), which spent roughly $42 million running a campaign against him during his hard-fought August Democratic primary victory over U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens. Celebrating his triumph, El-Sayed invoked the Arabic phrase "Alhamdulillah," which translates to "Praise be to God." Students told Fox News Digital that young voters were looking for tangible change over empty promises. EL-SAYED MOCKS TRUMP, VANCE AND ROGERS IN GLOATING VICTORY SPEECH SIGNALING COMBATIVE TONE IN SENATE "They're feeling happy because what they wanted is coming," one student named Hernandez said. "I just really hope that we actually see something, and it's not just nothing happens from this." The progressive senator-elect also took a sharp jab at his defeated opponent during his victory speech. "Enjoy your retirement," El-Sayed said of Rogers, the former Republican congressman. "You chose hate, and Michigan chose hope. May we never have to see the likes of you in this state again." Isabelle, a junior studying movement science, echoed El-Sayed’s sentiment, describing Rogers’ platform as hostile. "I feel like [El-Sayed] ran a very good election, and the opponent's policies tended to be a lot more full of hate and less inclusion for everyone here," she said. "The University of Michigan is a very inclusive university where that's really important, so I think that especially resonated with a lot of the students here." A staff member for the university noted that many students had felt anxious about their prospects for entering the workforce amid broader economic headwinds. TOP UNION BOSS DROPS 2028 WARNING ON DEMOCRATS AMID BLUE WAVE CELEBRATION: 'WAKE-UP CALL' "I think students are kind of scared of the future. They're here to plan their lives and enter into the real world," said Stephanie Brooks, a staff member for the School for Environment and Sustainability. "I think a lot of them were really nervous in this current environment about what their future was going to look like. I think Abdul provided a lot of hope, security, and trust in that way." AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI Another student, Kabir, told Fox News Digital that cost-of-living issues played a major role in student turnout. "I think … what we see around the country in terms of rising prices and all that stuff, I think a progressive who promises things to our people that we want is going to be successful," Kabir said. OBAMA PREPARES TO RALLY WITH MICHIGAN DEM WHO ONCE DELIVERED SCATHING VERDICT ON HIS PRESIDENCY Students also pointed to El-Sayed’s local ties as a major factor in driving campus engagement. El-Sayed earned his undergraduate degree from the University of Michigan in 2007. "I love Abdul El-Sayed," Shaik said. "Being a Michigan alumnus feels really nice. He was around campus the other day and I got a chance to meet him. It feels good to be around someone who feels very close and connected with." articles.title: The many winning strategies of Democrats
articles.summary: A former governor in North Carolina. A Methodist pastor in Kansas. A progressive doctor in Michigan.
articles.body: A former governor in North Carolina. A Methodist pastor in Kansas. A progressive doctor in Michigan. Democrats have assembled a winning coalition whose candidates offer different answers to the question now facing the party: what exactly have Americans voted for?Roy Cooper brought two terms as governor to his North Carolina Senate campaign. Adam Hamilton’s Kansas victory drew on the standing of a prominent religious leader. Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan after securing the backing of progressive leaders, including Bernie Sanders. There was more than one route through Republican defences.Local Credibility Travelled FurtherThe tempting conclusion is that Democrats have discovered a single national formula. The evidence points instead towards candidates adapting to their states.In Texas, James Talarico combined an economic message with religious language, while moderating positions on some contentious social issues. Hamilton presented himself to Kansas voters as an independent-minded Democrat.These approaches gave voters ways to support an opposition candidate without necessarily embracing every position associated with the national party.That matters for Democrats’ next election.Rejection Easier Than AgreementThe AP Voter Poll found Democrats held at least modest advantages on handling the economy and corruption. Yet the party was not substantially more popular than the Republicans. Its victory therefore cannot be read as approval for an unrestricted Democratic programme.Members elected from Republican-leaning territory will have particular reason to demonstrate practical results. Others will face pressure from supporters demanding investigations and a more combative opposition.Choosing FightsDemocrats must decide which measures are worth negotiating with Trump and which are intended to expose differences before 2028. articles.summary: At a chapel in Lindsborg, Kansas, Adam Hamilton began singing a hymn. The audience joined in.
articles.body: At a chapel in Lindsborg, Kansas, Adam Hamilton began singing a hymn. The audience joined in. The Methodist pastor was seeking votes for the US Senate, carrying a pocket Bible and a chunk of salt, a reminder of Jesus’ Sermon on the Mount.Hamilton, a former Republican running as a Democrat, offered a gentle pitch in a bitter campaign. “Most of us... are not enemies. If we’re liberals or conservatives, we just see the world differently,” he said.There were signs that Republicans were listening. Bruce Bratman, who had voted for Trump three times, said he was knocking on doors for Hamilton. At another stop, retired Kroger chief executive Dave Dillon, a registered Republican, endorsed the Democrat.Hamilton defeated Republican Senator Roger Marshall, ending a Democratic Senate drought stretching to 1932.His campaign offered one answer to a difficult question: how to ask people to change their vote without asking them to change who they are.You use AI every day. articles.title: Oversight layer intact, says EC official after poll panel tweaks work order for IT chief Seema Khanna
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Election Commission on Thursday said there is no change in the supervisory authority to which its director general of information
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Election Commission on Thursday said there is no change in the supervisory authority to which its director general of information technology Seema Khanna reports.The clarification came a day after the panel issued a fresh work allocation placing Khanna under the charge of deputy election commissioner Prakash Raj Purohit instead of senior deputy EC Manish Garg.A controversy had erupted after Garg issued an order on July 28 asking Khanna to report directly to the Election Commission, comprising Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and Election Commissioners Vivek Joshi and SS Sandhu.Garg had issued the order after deputy EC Sanjay Kumar, to whom Khanna had been reporting, was transferred to the Delhi government. The change effectively removed an intermediary layer of oversight, allowing Khanna to report directly to the Election Commission.ECs Sandhu and Joshi objected to the order and subsequently wrote separate letters to cabinet secretary TV Somanathan, raising concerns over the distribution of responsibilities. The order was then put in abeyance. The EC also told the Supreme Court that the July 28 work allocation order was never implemented.Asked whether Khanna had reported directly to the Commission between July 28 and November 4, without an added layer of a reporting boss in the form of a deputy EC, an election official on Thursday said: "Since the order was not implemented, Khanna was supervised by Garg after Sanjay Kumar moved out of the EC. Now, she will report to Raj Purohit, who joined as deputy EC a few days ago."Garg was the "link officer" for Kumar, which meant that Kumar's assigned tasks were transferred to Garg after he left the Election Commission.Why was Seema Khanna's role under scrutiny?Khanna's role had come under scrutiny amid concerns over the functioning of the electoral roll software and the exercise of powers by Electoral Registration Officers (EROs).According to a report by The Indian Express, the two Election Commissioners were concerned that field-level officers, who are legally responsible for preparing electoral rolls, were unable to perform certain functions because the software did not permit them to do so.The permissions required to carry out these functions were reportedly controlled by the EC's IT division, headed by Khanna.The commissioners repeatedly raised concerns that powers legally vested in EROs were being increasingly centralised through the EC's IT system, potentially restricting the authority of officers responsible for preparing and revising electoral rolls.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Sir Tom Jones tells fans he thought life 'was over' after flu
articles.summary: The singer from Pontypridd told the audience just how serious his "bad case of the flu" was.
articles.body:
Sir Tom Jones has told fans he feared his life was "over" after being admitted to hospital in the US with flu.

The 86-year-old from Pontypridd spent a week at the Ronald Regan UCLA Medical Center in Los Angeles and was forced to cancel or reschedule a number of concerts.

But on Wednesday night, he was back on stage at the Greek Theatre and told the audience just how serious his "bad case of the flu" was.

"[I thought] Oh well, this is it, you've had a wonderful life, Tommy, but it's over right now," he said.

"I must say this, in the UCLA, they really did a wonderful job. So I'm here."

"[The medical staff said] What do you want to do now? I was in there for a week. And I said, 'I've got to get back on the stage'. This is where I belong. I can't live without this, believe me."

Sir Tom recently made headlines after revealing ITV had "made the decision" to "fire" him from The Voice UK coaching panel , having served as an coach on the singing competition since its debut in 2012.

In the latest series, and his last as a coach, he mentored Welsh singer Cate McHugh to victory .

McHugh previously told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast that being chosen to be on Team Tom at the blind audition was "absolutely undescribable".

The Delilah and It's Not Unusual singer has achieved three UK number one singles and four chart-topping albums during a music career spanning more than six decades.

His awards include one Grammy and two Brits, and in 2006 he received a knighthood from the late Queen Elizabeth II for services to music.

He is next due to perform at the Yaamava' Theater in San Bernadino, California on Friday.

articles.title: Could the US midterms further isolate Israel in Washington?
articles.summary: The midterms showed that challenging support for Israel can win votes. But changing US foreign policy may be harder.
articles.body:
As the midterm votes trickled in on Tuesday and Democrats locked up majorities in both chambers of the United States Congress, Republicans began pointing fingers at the Trump administration’s increasingly unpopular foreign policies.

“The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone,” Vice President JD Vance said on X, blaming the war on Iran, which has triggered soaring fuel prices and a $47bn bill, for souring voters on the Republican Party. Many, already appalled at US-funded Israeli genocide in Gaza and the occupation of southern Lebanon, also view the Trump administration as having been convinced to launch strikes on Iran on February 28 by Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu government, which insisted without evidence that Iran was “close” to developing a nuclear weapon.

An unnamed pollster, Vance said, had asked voters who had switched parties for this election what would bring them back. Summing up the causes for their displeasure with Trump’s government, they said they wanted an end to the war on Iran, action on the cost of living, a return to “America First” and a fundamental change in Washington’s relationship with Israel.

All of it, voters say, went directly against Trump’s campaign promises to end the US involvement in foreign wars and to bring down the cost of living.

About six in 10 voters surveyed by The Associated Press said that going to war with Iran was the wrong decision. Even more called the cost of living key to their decision about how to vote in the midterm elections. “Voters may not have been thinking about the specific details of the conflict, but they connected the war with the rise of the cost of living in the United States, and punished Republicans for it,” Andrew Payne of the Chatham House think tank told Al Jazeera.

Meanwhile in Detroit, Michigan’s Democratic senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed had called for an end to US military assistance to Israel, a position that experts say echoed the “America First” message on which many Republicans had won previous midterm races. He won his contest despite a vigorous campaign by the Republicans, and funded by the deep-pocketed, pro-Israel AIPAC lobby group. Although El-Sayed’s campaign focused primarily on healthcare and the cost of living, it may have been anger towards Israel that propelled the first Muslim into the US Senate.

“We don’t want our money sent to do apartheid or genocide or war,” El-Sayed told supporters from the podium, where he also took a jab at Vance. The two politicians sit at opposite ends of the political spectrum, but Vance’s diagnosis signals, at the very least, a rift in the Republican alliance with Netanyahu.

Payne said he believes a broader Republican realignment remains unlikely at this stage. But with Democrats winning so handily and criticism of Israel front and centre in some of their biggest swing-state upsets, he said that “the party could be emboldened to take an even tougher line moving forward.”

“There are very few issues on which we’ll see such a stark partisan contrast, making it one of the most likely to cut through in the presidential campaign in 2028,” Payne said.

On Wednesday night, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), the major US pro-Israel lobby which raises funds in support of pro-Israel political candidates , claimed more than “234 candidates” supported by its members had won their seats.

The group’s post on X congratulated Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries, the two Democratic leaders, as a swift reminder that it maintains support from both parties.

But the picture looks worse for AIPAC when measured by where its money went. A Responsible Statecraft report has found that AIPAC’s super PAC, United Democracy Project (UDP), and several other political committees spent $84.1m on races. Of that, $55.3m went on races where their preferred candidate lost. In 2022 and 2024, by comparison, 69 percent and 87 percent of UDP’s spending went to races where its preferred candidates won.

It was Abdul El-Sayed’s Michigan race that proved to be the Israeli lobby’s most expensive setback. Responsible Statecraft put UDP’s spending on efforts to defeat El-Sayed at $31.47m across the primary and general election campaign periods. El-Sayed won both, and for Democrats weighing whether to challenge the party’s position on Israel, his victory establishes a strong precedent in which a candidate called for an end to military aid to Israel, withstood heavy outside donor spending and still won a statewide race in a swing state that Trump won in 2024.

Trump himself had already signalled that he understood the political cost. On election day, he said Washington would end annual military aid to Israel after this year, taking away what he called a “bad talking point” for Democrats. The existing agreement provides for $3.8bn a year through September 2028. Trump offered few details about how he would bring an early end to the funding and said the US would keep selling Israel weapons, prompting scepticism from observers.

What, if anything, could change for Gaza now?

Once Democrats take control of both houses, they are likely to use committee hearings and investigations to probe what both the Biden and Trump administrations knew about how Israel was using US weapons in Gaza, and why weapon transfers continued amid allegations of grave violations of international law, experts told Al Jazeera. Lawmakers can also seek conditions for future military funding and force votes on individual sales.

The appetite for such votes has grown over time. In January 2024, 11 senators backed an effort by Senator Bernie Sanders to require the US Department of State to report on Israel’s human rights record. A motion to advance a measure blocking a weapons sale drew 27 in July 2025. In April this year, 40 senators voted to advance a measure opposing a sale of military bulldozers to Israel, and 36 backed a similar move on 1,000-pound bombs.

A Democratic majority could possibly tip the balance in favour of some sort of partial ban on weapons sales. But Daniel Levy, president of the US/ Middle East Project (USMEP) and a former Israeli peace negotiator, told Al Jazeera that would likely be upended by Trump’s use of the presidential veto. On Tuesday, Trump told Fox News he plans to use the veto to block “insane” Democratic policies in Congress. Overriding a veto requires a two-thirds majority in both houses of Congress, which the Democrats are unlikely to be able to secure.

“I would not underestimate the extent to which executive privilege can be deployed in the ways this administration has deployed it, approaching and crossing lines that the US system of checks and balances should have enforced, but hasn’t,” Levy said.

Congress can put US support for Israel under greater scrutiny, but analysts say unpicking the security ties that bind the two countries will be a lot trickier.

“We might start to see a tougher line, but there are deeper structural issues at play that transcend Congress,” said Simon Mabon, a professor of international politics at Lancaster University. “They are tied to US institutions and other parts of the government, including military collaboration.”

“Democrats might start to capitalise on waning public support for Israel, but there are limits to what they can do,” Mabon said.

Since the Republican defeat this week, AIPAC has told its members it is “determined to expand political activism in the cycles ahead”.

Levy said that “the Israel lobby can still spend enough to keep lawmakers on board, and if ties in technology, AI, military AI and the wider economy hold, Israel may be able to ride out much of the pressure for change.”

He added that much of the lobby may also present dwindling support for Israel as a problem with Netanyahu or with far-right figures such as Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, rather than the Israeli state’s almost cross-party support for the war with Iran and strikes on Gaza.

Former Israeli Prime Minister Yair Lapid attempted a version of that argument on X on Wednesday. “These people aren’t against Israel. They’re against extremist ministers who say crazy things. They’re against settler violence; they’re against a government they don’t understand; they’re mainly against Netanyahu – for them, anything connected to him is toxic.”

He also faulted Netanyahu for openly siding with Republicans and urged the next Israeli government to meet both parties in Congress and hear their criticisms. He hopes a new, more liberal, government in Israel could reopen the closing doors with Washington’s lawmakers.

But the harder task would be persuading voters who object to US support for the genocide in Gaza and the Iran war, that changing Israel’s leadership would change those policies.

“Many voters believe the [Iran] war took place at Israel’s behest and would not have happened without Israel dragging the United States into it,” Levy said.

Analysts say it is unclear whether this will translate into policies that materially change the course of Israel’s genocidal policy in Gaza. What is clear is that this has been a bad election for Israel, as criticism of the country gains ground and moves into mainstream US political debate.

“For many voters, particularly Democrats, it also comes after several years of what they see as US complicity in the horrors of Israel’s war on Gaza,” Levy added.

articles.title: ‘Healthcare not bombs’: How Gaza shaped Adam Hamawy’s path to US Congress
articles.summary: Former army surgeon and Gaza volunteer Hamawy is the first Muslim American elected to the US Congress from New Jersey.
articles.body:
Adam Hamawy has seen death, devastation and the effects of hate on others for decades – as a first responder after the September 11 attacks, while serving in Iraq as a United States military surgeon, and more recently, on trips to Gaza while it has suffered under Israel’s genocide.

On Tuesday, he stood in front of supporters in Plainsboro, New Jersey, celebrating “hope” that he said he had gleaned from some of those victims of violence.

“To the men, women and children of Gaza and Palestine: Your smiles give me the hope and the courage to fight for a better world,” said the Egyptian-American surgeon, set to become New Jersey’s first Muslim US congressman.

It was the culmination of a winding path into politics for 56-year-old Hamawy, a US Army veteran and reconstructive surgeon who was one of eight Muslim Americans to win election races on Tuesday night, as Democrats took commanding control of both chambers of the US Congress .

Hamawy entered politics after participating in medical missions to Gaza in 2024 and 2025, experiences he said made it impossible for him to return to normal life.

He campaigned for New Jersey’s 12th Congressional District on a platform of “healthcare not bombs”, pledging to challenge a system that “funds genocide [in Gaza] while trapping us all here in medical debt”.

But Hamawy’s bid for the House of Representatives was met with a wave of attacks that he described as “anti-Muslim”, as well as scrutiny over his past association with a sheikh later convicted of seditious conspiracy.

“I have never seen anti-Muslim hate as open and as loud and as accepted as it is today,” said Hamawy, who served for eight years as a US Army officer, including a deployment to Iraq as a combat surgeon.

“Let me say this to anyone who still believes that Muslims are strangers here. To every Muslim child who’s been told that you don’t belong: You belong,” he said.

The American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee (ADC) welcomed Hamawy’s victory, along with those of other “principled candidates”.

“Hamawy witnessed the horrors of Israel’s genocide in Gaza firsthand,” the ADC said. “Now, he will take his place in the very Congress that funded and enabled those atrocities, bringing the testimony of what he witnessed directly to the lawmakers responsible for sustaining US support for Israel’s genocide.”

Hamawy was born in Egypt, and his family moved to New Jersey when he was a baby. Raised in Old Bridge, New Jersey, Hamawy completed his undergraduate studies at Rutgers University and earned a medical degree from New Jersey Medical School.

He later joined the New Jersey National Guard and worked as a combat trauma surgeon for the US Army, including on a nine-month deployment to Baghdad, Iraq in 2004.

It was there that Hamawy treated now-Illinois Senator Tammy Duckworth , who at the time was a US Army helicopter pilot. Duckworth was badly injured when her helicopter was shot down by Iraqi fighters in November 2004, and says Hamawy saved her life and one of her limbs.

“He is the doctor who not only saved my life, but was able to prevent me from becoming a triple amputee by employing a vascular procedure that he’d just learned in medical school,” said Duckworth, who lost both her legs.

The Illinois senator was the first serving US congressperson to endorse Hamawy back in January, calling him a leader with the courage to “speak truth to power” and “willingness to call out injustices at home and abroad”.

Hamawy retired from the army with the rank of lieutenant colonel in 2011. In the years leading up to and following his retirement, he put his medical skills to use in numerous humanitarian missions abroad, including treating victims of war and disaster in Haiti, Jordan, Lebanon and Gaza.

During Hamawy’s first mission to Gaza in 2024, he said the level of destruction was unlike anything he had ever seen before.

“This is not like a war. This is just like complete, utter destruction,” said Hamawy in an interview from the enclave, adding that he could only define what was happening there “as a genocide”.

“When the hospital shakes and I see the bodies come in, I’m paying for it with my tax dollars,” he later said in an interview with The Guardian. “I don’t want my tax dollars doing that.”

While he treated patients at Gaza’s European Hospital in 2024, Israel seized the Rafah border crossing , temporarily trapping Hamawy and his colleagues in the enclave. Hamawy refused to be evacuated until he was assured non-American members of his team would also be able to leave.

Hamawy declared his congressional candidacy in January after the retirement announcement of Representative Bonnie Watson Coleman. He quickly faced fierce criticism from opponents, including Democratic challenger Adrian Mapp, who called him a “radical extremist”.

Mapp and other critics pointed to Hamawy’s past association with Omar Abdel Rahman, known as the “Blind Sheikh” , who was later convicted of several “terrorism” charges, including in connection with the 1993 World Trade Center bombing. Hamawy, in his early 20s, travelled to a conference with Abdel Rahman and others and later was called as a defence witness at Abdel Rahman’s trial.

Hawamy has condemned Abdel Rahman’s “violent rhetoric and actions” and says he testified at his trial out of a sense of “civic duty”.

Still, several New Jersey politicians accused Hamawy of failing to answer for his connection to Abdel Rahman, who died in 2017.

“As a Muslim, they’re always going to find something to attack,” Hamawy told local media earlier this year, as his campaign called the scrutiny “gross and bigoted”.

After winning his congressional race, Hamawy said the hate he had faced had also been “targeted against my family, my coworkers, my friends”, and that his “loyalty” and “patriotism” had been questioned.

Selaedin Maksut, executive director of the New Jersey chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, said, “Islamophobic rhetoric employed by so many candidates miserably backfired this election season.”

“New Jersey is a better place because American Muslims are standing up, speaking out, and fighting for a more just future for all,” said Maksut.

Hamawy’s platform priorities included healthcare for all, ending medical and student debt, and abolishing US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which he has called an agency “full of neo-Nazis”.

He has said the push for universal healthcare is personal for him, as a physician “who sees firsthand how insurance companies and the rest of our absurd system fail patients and providers alike”.

On foreign policy, Hamawy opposes the war on Iran, which he has called “illegal and immoral”, and advocates an end to US military aid to Israel. He has pledged to fight for “for justice and equal rights for Palestinians, including support for the Palestinian right of return under international law”.

The surgeon-turned-congressman has described his policy goals as “interconnected”.

“They are solutions to a crisis that was born out of a broken and rigged political and economical system,” he said after winning a hard-fought Democratic primary race in June.

“A system that floods money overseas to bomb children’s schools while at the same time [saying] that childcare here in America [is a] pie-in-the-sky idea.”

articles.title: Increase to Alderney air links subsidy rejected
articles.summary: Alderney representatives wanted to bring the subsidy up to £1.86m from £1.5m
articles.body:
Politicians have voted to keep the public subsidy for an island's air links at £1.5m for 2027.

Alderney's representative to the States of Guernsey asked for an extra £364,000 to bring the funding to a minimum of £1.86m, but it was dismissed with 10 deputies voting in favour and 23 voting against.

Alex Snowdon, Alderney States member and representative to Guernsey, said an action plan needed to be drawn up to address the "urgent crisis of aviation services in Alderney".

Policy & Resources vice-president, Yvonne Burford, said the committee had budgeted £1.7m, an extra £200,000, in light of high fuel prices due to the US-Israel war with Iran.

In his speech, Alderney representative Edward Hill said disruption to Alderney's links was impacting on some residents' cancer treatments.

He said: "I had breakfast with a lady this morning who had come over for cancer treatment, she told me her oncologist had told her that they are very, very reluctant to enter into certain forms of chemotherapy for Alderney patients because of the necessary need to have chronological timing guarantees."

Snowdon said things needed to move forward "rapidly" or things would get worse.

"This isn't going away anytime soon," he said.

"I do think there needs to be urgent action between the States of Guernsey and States of Alderney to look for some sort of solution to improve things or it is going to cost everyone a lot more money."

Reacting after the decision, Snowdon said the governments' emergency response body, the Civil Contingencies Authority, may need to get involved.

"People's lives are really important," he said.

"People needing cancer treatments, people needing treatment in Guernsey for all different sorts of situations, if the planes aren't flying because of technical or not having enough crew something is seriously wrong.

"I urge the States of Deliberation to start taking some appropriate action to resolve this."

articles.title: Why Guinea-Bissau halted a controversial hepatitis vaccine trial for babies
articles.summary: Experts have said the US-funded trial would deny critical vaccines to thousands of infants.
articles.body:
Guinea-Bissau has reportedly halted a controversial United States-funded hepatitis B virus vaccine (HBV) trial which drew global scrutiny when experts said it involved withholding lifesaving shots from thousands of babies.

The trial failed to gain the necessary government approval, one researcher involved in the project said in a statement, adding that the end of the trial was a “significant setback” for African science.

The West African nation’s judicial police said in mid-October that it had raided the facilities of the research group leading the project in the capital, Bissau, and seized vaccine batches.

Authorities said inquiries were continuing to determine whether the trial had complied with the country’s safety standards.

The trial was designed to assess the effects of World Health Organization (WHO)-recommended HBV vaccines on two groups of babies. One group would receive the vaccine at birth, and another, chosen at random, would receive it six weeks later.

Some 14,000 babies were expected to be involved in the trial. The researchers planned to assess health outcomes over five years for the two sets.

The project secured $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) under Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy, who has previously made his anti-vaccine views known.

However, the announcement of the trial in December last year met with widespread anger over the withholding of the vaccine from one set of babies. In January, the Guinea-Bissau government paused the project and launched a review.

The Danish research group, Bissau-based Bandim Health Project, part of the University of Southern Denmark, planned the trial.

It is chaired by prominent scientists Christine Stabell Benn and Peter Aaby, a married couple. Since 1978, they have run the Bandim Health Project out of Bissau and have conducted studies on thousands of Bissau-Guineans.

Both researchers primarily study unintended impacts of vaccines and have theorised that vaccines which contain inactivated viruses can cause death, including the HBV vaccine which they planned to test in Bissau.

Their counterparts in Denmark have, however, repeatedly accused them of downplaying trial results or withholding evidence that does not align with their narrative.

One of the pair’s studies found that WHO-approved vaccines against diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis (DTP) led to higher infant deaths, especially for girls. WHO said the pair’s study was inconsistent but merited further review, and advised countries to keep vaccinating babies.

Last February, investigations by the Danish publication, Weekendavisen, found that the researchers had not publicised the null results of one of their randomised controlled trials (RCTs) on the DTP vaccine conducted 14 years ago. The study was published after the expose.

Why is the hepatitis B trial controversial?

In this case, health experts questioned the morality of withholding a highly effective vaccine from thousands of babies for the purposes of research. WHO called it “unethical”.

Infants are at the highest risk of being chronically infected with hepatitis B – usually passed to them from their mothers. The disease has no cure and can lead to long-term liver damage and cancer. WHO recommends HBV vaccines at birth for all babies, as well as booster shots, which are known to offer years of protection.

Guinea-Bissau has one of the highest numbers of people living with hepatitis B – one-fifth of the 2.2 million population. Because it cannot access enough doses, the government authorises the vaccine at up to six weeks after birth. However, it is working to start at-birth hepatitis B vaccination for all babies from 2028.

The researchers argued that the timeframe between now and 2028 provides a “unique window of opportunity” to assess how the vaccine affects babies who receive it at birth against those who receive it after six weeks. They noted that the research would see thousands of babies receive the shot at birth before the official schedule kicks in.

But health experts pushed back, saying the study would essentially hold back vaccines from the other half who would have had access to it if the government in Bissau could afford it. They said the effects, if some babies do develop hepatitis B, could last for a lifetime.

“[The researchers] took advantage of the fact that Guinea-Bissau does not have a very strong research capacity … a very strong critical mass of public health professionals, very well vested in understanding what the politics that surround global health are,” Magda Robalo, a former Guinea-Bissau health minister, told Al Jazeera.

“It is unethical to deny children an intervention that we know works, that will contribute to improving their lives and save them from a disease that we know they will likely acquire,” she added.

Some also questioned why the researchers planned to make the trial “open label”, meaning the researchers would know which participants received the vaccines, and when. Such randomised trials are usually conducted “blind”.

Others pointed out that the trial is reminiscent of the Tuskegee trial in Alabama, US, which saw health authorities study effects of untreated syphilis in Black men between 1932 and 1972, even though penicillin treatments were available at the time. More than 100 men died.

Benn denied any wrongdoing in the group’s work in an email to Al Jazeera in February this year.

In a joint statement, Benn and Aaby further clarified that they were not testing whether the HBV vaccine prevents the disease, but “whether the prevention [of the disease] comes at a prohibitive price”, such as death and other health outcomes.

They accused their critics of lacking curiosity and a “humble” mindset, and said the research would add to a scientific body of work on the topic.

Guinea-Bissau launched an inquiry into the trial in conjunction with the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) and the WHO in January.

Officials also claimed the country’s transitional government, which took power following a November coup, had not been involved in the approval process.

A Danish ethics committee investigating the issue separately reportedly received information that Guinea-Bissau had approved an updated proposal, causing its members to vote that the project continue.

However, Health Minister Quinhin Nantote denied that report in a media statement in mid-October, following a meeting with the researchers and local health agencies.

On October 19, police raided and seized batches of the vaccine from Bandim facilities. Authorities also appear to have cancelled the trial.

“It is now clear that the hepatitis B-NSE trial will not move forward in Guinea-Bissau – we were not given the necessary governmental approval, Bandim researcher Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer said in a LinkedIn post a few days later.

articles.title: Owners of seized Russian oil tanker claim U.S. improperly sold ship for scrap metal
articles.summary: U.S. authorities sold a seized Russian oil tanker to a maritime scrap dealer for well under market value in an “economically irrational” deal meant to thwart the owner’s bid to recover the vessel, the company lawyers said in court papers.
articles.body: U.S. authorities sold a seized Russian oil tanker to a maritime scrap dealer for well under market value in an “economically irrational” deal meant to thwart the owner’s bid to recover the vessel, the company lawyers said in court papers. The Justice Department was ordered to respond to the allegations, made by the ship’s Russian owner, Burevestmarin LLC, by 9 a.m. Friday. The tanker, Bella 1, was seized by the U.S. military in the North Atlantic in early January after a weekslong chase on the high seas. U.S. authorities said the ship, which they believed was carrying illegal Iranian oil, was caught fleeing an American blockade of Venezuela. Attorneys for Burevestmarin dispute the claim that the vessel was carrying Iranian oil. The ship was sold to a scrap dealer for $9.1 million, the company’s lawyers said, well below the $21 million that the Bella 1 would fetch as scrap metal alone. Even a proper scrap metal price tag would understate its worth, they added, because the ship has “substantially greater value” as “an operating commercial vessel.” “As discussed and previously briefed, the Government posits a world in which it can — while withholding notice to known interested parties and while aware of challenges to the Court’s jurisdiction — engage in precisely this kind of economically irrational sale for its own convenience,” the owner’s lawyers wrote. They said the sale was conducted “behind closed doors” as part of the government’s “self-interested and unreasonable decisions.” Representatives for the Justice Department and the scrap dealer named in court documents could not be immediately reached for comment Thursday.

articles.title: Photos: Spain mourns Jesus de Miguel, who died after on-pitch collision
articles.summary: Mourners gather in Navahermosa to honour Tenerife player, whose death has united Spain’s football community in grief.
articles.body:
Spain’s national football team coach and the president of Real Madrid joined family, friends and teammates on Thursday at the funeral of Jesus de Miguel , the Tenerife player who died after an on‑field collision earlier this week.

The service was held in Navahermosa, a town of about 3,000 people in central Spain, where De Miguel’s parents were reportedly born.

A hearse covered in flowers moved slowly towards the church as dozens of mourners, some carrying candles, walked behind. The town hall declared three days of mourning, with flags at half-staff.

De Miguel, 30, suffered cardiac arrest after colliding with Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono while challenging for a high ball during a second‑division match on Monday. He died in hospital the following day.

Spain coach Luis de la Fuente and Real Madrid President Florentino Perez attended the funeral, with De la Fuente saying the game’s community “stands united” in grief.

Police have opened a routine investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter to assess whether the challenge went beyond normal play.

Tributes have poured in from clubs across Europe, with De Miguel’s death described as a rare and shocking tragedy in professional football.
